subject: Medicine
summary: Aortic stenosis is a progressive narrowing of the aortic valve that limits blood flow from the left ventricle, causing symptoms of angina, syncope, and heart failure. It is most common in the elderly due to calcific degeneration, but can also arise from bicuspid valves or rheumatic disease.

sections.p: Aortic stenosis (AS) is defined by a valve area <1.0 cm² or a mean gradient >40 mmHg on echocardiography. The classic murmur is a harsh systolic ejection sound at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids.
b: Valve area <1.0 cm² or mean gradient >40 mmHg

t.b: Measures valve area, gradients, and ventricular function; confirms AS severity.
Shows left ventricular hypertrophy and aortic root enlargement; suggests chronic pressure overload.
Detects LV hypertrophy, conduction delays, and arrhythmias that may accompany AS.

sections.p: Severity is staged by valve area and mean gradient: mild (1.0–1.5 cm², 20–39 mmHg), moderate (0.75–1.0 cm², 40–59 mmHg), severe (<0.75 cm², ≥60 mmHg).
In developed settings, age‑related calcific degeneration is first. In younger patients, bicuspid aortic valve is common. Rheumatic fever remains a major cause in low‑resource areas.

Patients often report exertional chest pain, fainting spells, and shortness of breath. Physical exam reveals a crescendo‑decrescendo systolic murmur, a delayed carotid upstroke, and a narrow pulse pressure.
Echocardiography is the gold standard. When unavailable, a focused cardiac exam and ECG can suggest AS, but confirmatory imaging is essential.

t.b: Quantifies valve area, gradients, and LV function; defines severity.
Provides detailed valve morphology when echo is suboptimal.
Assesses aortic valve calcification burden; useful when echo is equivocal.

sections.p: Uncontrolled hypertension, new arrhythmias, or worsening dyspnea signal impending heart failure or sudden death. Syncope, especially on exertion, is an urgent red flag.

Treat reversible causes first. Long‑term, beta‑blockers or calcium‑channel blockers relieve angina but avoid excessive vasodilation. Definitive therapy is valve replacement (surgical or transcatheter).
b: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) for high‑risk patients

sections.p: Regular echocardiographic surveillance every 1–2 years in asymptomatic severe AS. Prevent rheumatic fever with prompt streptococcal treatment and secondary prophylaxis.
b: Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce infection risk

sections.p: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic regurgitation, and pulmonary hypertension can mimic AS symptoms but have different murmurs and hemodynamics.
b: Pulmonary hypertension – right‑sided murmur, elevated JVP

sections.p: A normal ECG does not exclude AS; LV hypertrophy may be subtle. A low‑grade murmur can be missed in early disease. Echo may underestimate severity if loading conditions are altered.

faq.q: What is the classic murmur of aortic stenosis?
faq.a: A harsh crescendo‑decrescendo systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids.
Yes, many patients remain asymptomatic until severe, but they may still have a murmur and LV hypertrophy.

faq.q: Why is beta‑blocker therapy used in AS?
faq.a: It reduces heart rate, prolongs diastole, and improves coronary perfusion, relieving angina without causing severe hypotension.

exam: Explain the diagnostic criteria for severe aortic stenosis and why a valve area <0.75 cm² is critical.
Describe the clinical triad of aortic stenosis and how each symptom reflects underlying pathophysiology.
Outline the management pathway for a 70‑year‑old patient with severe AS and new atrial fibrillation in a low‑resource setting.
